## Short version

A TLB is a small CPU cache that stores recent address translations. On a big-memory server, many random accesses miss the TLB and need several extra memory reads. Huge pages make each entry cover 512 times more memory, with risks of wasted memory and long pauses.

## Words used here

- **Page**: the unit of memory mapping. The x86-64 default size is 4 KiB.
- **TLB (translation lookaside buffer)**: a cache inside the CPU. Each entry holds the translation for one page.
- **Page table**: the tables in memory that hold every translation. x86-64 uses 4 levels [Ref1].
- **Page walk**: the CPU reads the page table after a TLB miss.
- **TLB reach**: the amount of memory that all TLB entries cover together.
- **Huge page**: a page of 2 MiB or 1 GiB on x86-64.
- **THP (transparent huge pages)**: the Linux feature that gives huge pages to programs automatically.
- **hugetlbfs**: the Linux feature that reserves huge pages for programs that request them.
- **madvise**: the system call that passes memory hints to the kernel.
- **NUMA (non-uniform memory access)**: a server design where each CPU socket has its own memory.
- **est.**: an estimate, not a measurement.

## 1. What a TLB is

- A program uses virtual addresses. The CPU must translate each one to a physical address.
- The full translation data is in the page table, in main memory.
- The TLB keeps the most recent translations inside the CPU.
- A TLB hit adds almost no time. A TLB miss starts a page walk.

```
virtual address --> TLB --hit--> physical address
                     |
                    miss
                     v
       page walk: level 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 --> physical address
       (up to 4 memory reads, then the TLB stores the result)
```

## 2. Why misses are expensive on a big-memory server

The numbers below assume a server with 512 GiB of RAM and a 2,048-entry TLB. That entry count is typical for recent server CPUs (est.). The `cpuid` tool prints the real count for your CPU.

- **The reach is small.** 2,048 entries of 4 KiB cover 8 MiB. That is 0.0015% of 512 GiB.
- **Each miss needs several memory reads.** A page walk reads up to 4 table entries [Ref1].
- **The last read is slow.** The last-level tables for 512 GiB take 1 GiB, more than the CPU caches hold. So that read often goes to main memory. One such read costs about 100 ns (est.), 300 cycles at 3 GHz.
- **Virtual machines add more reads.** Inside a virtual machine, one walk can need up to 24 memory reads [Ref2].
- **NUMA adds distance.** The page table can be located on another socket. A read from another socket takes longer.
- **Measured cost.** One study of big-memory workloads measured up to 10% of CPU cycles spent on TLB misses [Ref3]. That figure was with huge pages already on.

The cost is highest for workloads that access a large memory range at random:

- hash tables
- graph traversal
- in-memory databases

Sequential access misses far less often. It needs one translation per 4 KiB of data.

## 3. How huge pages help

| Page size | Reach of 2,048 entries | Last-level tables for 512 GiB | Reads per walk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 KiB | 8 MiB (0.0015% of RAM) | 1 GiB | up to 4 |
| 2 MiB | 4 GiB (0.78% of RAM) | 2 MiB | up to 3 |
| 1 GiB | depends on the CPU (see section 4) | 4 KiB | up to 2 |

- **Fewer misses.** With 2 MiB pages, one entry covers 512 times more memory.
- **Cheaper misses.** The walk is one level shorter. The tables shrink from 1 GiB to 2 MiB. That size fits in the CPU caches.
- **Fewer page faults.** One fault maps 2 MiB. With 4 KiB pages the same range needs 512 faults.

Huge pages do not remove all misses. A 4 GiB reach is still under 1% of 512 GiB.

Linux offers two ways to get huge pages:

| | THP | hugetlbfs |
|---|---|---|
| Who chooses | the kernel, or the program through `madvise` | the program asks explicitly |
| Page sizes | 2 MiB | 2 MiB and 1 GiB |
| Guarantee | none, the kernel may use 4 KiB pages | yes, after the reservation succeeds |
| Unused memory | is released to the system | stays reserved |

## 4. What can go wrong

**With THP**

- **Memory use grows.** A program touches 1 byte. The kernel can then back it with a full 2 MiB page.
- **Long pauses at allocation.** The kernel may first move memory to build a free 2 MiB block. With the THP setting `defrag=always`, the program waits for that work [Ref4].
- **Results vary between runs.** After long uptime, free memory is split into small pieces. The kernel then uses 4 KiB pages and reports no error.
- **Background work at unplanned times.** The kernel thread khugepaged merges 4 KiB pages into huge pages later [Ref4]. It uses CPU time and holds locks on the memory map.
- **Slower fork.** After fork (the system call that copies a process), the first write to shared memory forces a copy. With huge pages each such write costs more. Redis advises turning THP off for this reason [Ref5].

A lower-risk THP setting is `enabled=madvise`. Then only programs that request huge pages get them [Ref4].

**With hugetlbfs**

- **Reserved memory is lost to all other use.** A reservation that is too large leaves too little memory for other programs. On a shared server this also affects other users.
- **A reservation that is too small makes the program fail.** The `mmap` call (the system call that maps memory) fails. In some cases the program gets SIGBUS (a fatal signal) at first access.
- **1 GiB pages need early reservation.** After long uptime, a free contiguous 1 GiB block is rare. So the kernel documentation advises reservation at boot [Ref6].
- **No swap.** The kernel cannot swap these pages out [Ref6].

**With both**

- **NUMA placement gets coarser.** One huge page is located on one socket. Threads on another socket then read remote memory.
- **The first access costs more.** The kernel clears the whole page before first use. Clearing 1 GiB takes about 100 ms (est.).
- **Some CPUs hold few 1 GiB entries.** Intel Skylake holds 16 of them in its second TLB level [Ref7]. That reach is 16 GiB, or 3.1% of 512 GiB.
- **No gain for some workloads.** A program with small memory use or sequential access gains little. Then only the risks remain.

## 5. Measurements that settle each point

- **Cost of misses today.** Run `perf stat -e dtlb_load_misses.walk_active,cycles` with perf (the Linux profiling tool) on an Intel CPU. The ratio is the share of cycles spent in page walks.
- **Huge pages really in use.** `AnonHugePages` in `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` shows the THP amount for one process.
- **Silent use of 4 KiB pages.** `thp_fault_fallback` in `/proc/vmstat` counts failed huge page allocations [Ref4].
- **Pauses.** `compact_stall` in `/proc/vmstat` counts waits for memory moves [Ref4].

## Limits of this answer

- I did not measure any machine for this answer.
- I cited the references from memory. I did not open them in this session.

## References

- [Ref1] Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 3A, chapter 4, "Paging".
- [Ref2] Bhargava et al., "Accelerating Two-Dimensional Page Walks for Virtualized Systems", ASPLOS 2008.
- [Ref3] Basu et al., "Efficient Virtual Memory for Big Memory Servers", ISCA 2013.
- [Ref4] Linux kernel documentation, "Transparent Hugepage Support", https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html
- [Ref5] Redis documentation, "Diagnosing latency issues", section on transparent huge pages.
- [Ref6] Linux kernel documentation, "HugeTLB Pages", https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/hugetlbpage.html
- [Ref7] Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Optimization Reference Manual, TLB parameters of the Skylake microarchitecture.
